answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Unusually for a viral Frida quote, this one is real and in her own hand. She wrote “Pies, ¿para qué los quiero si tengo alas para volar?” at the foot of a drawing in her personal diary in 1953, around the time her gangrenous right leg was amputated below the knee. The familiar English line is a faithful translation of that genuine Spanish original.

trail: Wikiquote lists the line in its sourced 1946–1953 quotations, citing a 1953 diary illustration reproduced on p. 415 of Hayden Herrera’s biography.
Spanish-language analyses trace it to a watercolour drawing in her personal diary, written the year before her death.
Reference sites such as LibQuotes likewise date it to the 1953 diary illustration preceding her amputation.

Both the original manuscript and the English translation are well after 1930 and remain in copyright; the diary is controlled by the Kahlo estate through Banco de México.

author.name: Frida Kahlo
author.heading: About Frida Kahlo
author.bio: Frida Kahlo was a Mexican painter known for her intensely personal self-portraits, drawn from a lifetime of physical suffering after a streetcar accident at eighteen left her with lasting injuries. In her final years she kept an illustrated diary, and in 1953 her right leg was amputated below the knee. It was beside a drawing in that diary that she wrote the defiant line about feet and wings — making this, unlike most quotes pinned to her name online, unmistakably her own words.

misattribution.heading: A rare genuine one — with caveats
misattribution.intro: Frida Kahlo is one of the internet’s biggest magnets for fabricated quotes, so the honest verdict here is a pleasant surprise: this line is authentically hers. The caveats are about wording and context, not authorship.

items.why: She wrote it in Spanish — “Pies, ¿para qué los quiero si tengo alas para volar?” The English “Feet, what do I need them for if I have wings to fly” is a faithful but later translation; punctuation and the question mark drift between versions online.

It circulates as a generic empowerment slogan, detached from its origin: a 1953 diary drawing written around her leg amputation. Whether she wrote it in resignation before surgery or defiance after is genuinely uncertain.

misattribution.truthLine: The attribution is correct: Wikiquote’s sourced section ties the line to her 1953 diary, reproduced in Hayden Herrera’s biography — a rare case where a viral Frida quote is truly hers.

context.heading: Why it endures
lead: The line lands so hard because of where it was written. By 1953 Frida Kahlo’s body was failing after decades of pain, and her right leg was removed below the knee to stop gangrene. Rather than record despair, she drew feet and wrote beneath them that she had no need of them — she had wings.

That is what separates this from the ocean of feel-good lines falsely pinned to her: it is not a stranger’s aphorism dressed in her face, but a sentence she actually set down in her own diary, in Spanish, at one of the darkest moments of her life.
